title: 2. What the Company Does: Segments, Revenue Mix & Concrete Examples
book_title: Chapter 2: Two Reportable Segments, Four Monetization Engines

epigraph.quote: A great platform monetizes the same attention twice: once from the consumer who values convenience, and once from the supplier who values discovery.
epigraph.author: Platform Economics Maxim

web_blocks.html: Spotify Technology S.A. reports results under two formal operating segments: Premium and Ad-Supported [1, 2]. Co-CEOs Alex Norström and Gustav Söderström monitor both lines jointly [1, 2]. Beneath those two reporting lines, the company runs four distinct economic engines [1, 2, 21, 22, 23]. These are Music & Lossless Subscriptions, Spoken-Word & Video Podcasts, Bundled & A-La-Carte Audiobooks, and the Two-Sided Artist Marketplace [1, 2, 21, 22, 23]. The Marketplace operates through Spotify Campaign Kit: Discovery Mode, Marquee, and Showcase [21, 22, 23]. Tracking how revenue and gross profit flow across these engines explains a 750-basis-point margin gain. Consolidated gross margin expanded from 25.6% in FY2023 to 33.1% in 9M 2026 [1, 2].

web_blocks.caption: Spotify Segment Revenue, Cost of Revenue & Gross Profit Mix (FY2023–9M 2026, € Millions)
web_blocks.takeaway: Premium generates 90.8% of revenue and 95.2% of gross profit (34.7% margin in 9M 2026), while Ad-Supported serves primarily as a top-of-funnel acquisition engine whose gross margin improved from 3.7% in FY2023 to 18.0% in FY2025 [1, 2].

web_blocks.html: 1. Premium Segment (90.8% of 9M 2026 Revenue; 34.7% Gross Margin): Premium delivers ad-free, on-demand, offline access to over 100 million music tracks [1, 2]. That catalog now includes 24-bit/44.1 kHz FLAC Lossless audio rolled out across 2025–2026 [1, 2, 25]. Subscribers also receive podcasts, including ad-free video podcasts under the 2025 Spotify Partner Program [1, 2]. Each Individual, Duo, Family, Student, or Basic plan includes 15 hours per month of audiobook listening [1, 2, 25]. Starting January 1, 2026, Spotify moved certain high-margin Marketplace and creator revenues into Premium [2]. That change aligns segment reporting with how the Co-CEOs manage the business [2]. Premium ARPU reached €4.95 in Q3 2026, up 9% YoY [2]. Pricing gains added €0.48 per user, partly offset by -€0.14 from emerging-market and plan-mix shifts [2].

Concrete End-to-End Example — Premium Subscriber & Audiobook/Lossless Bundle: Consider a U.S. Individual Premium subscriber paying $12.99/month, up from $9.99 prior to 2023 [21]. She streams 45 hours of music monthly, using AI DJ and daylist on her commute and 24-bit FLAC Lossless on her home hi-fi [25]. She also listens to 10 hours of a bestselling business audiobook from her 15-hour monthly allotment [25]. Because she uses that audiobook entitlement, Spotify allocates part of her fee to the audiobook vertical under its bundle valuation [1, 25]. That lowers the net music revenue base subject to U.S. statutory mechanical royalties, though the MLC's amended lawsuit continues to contest that allocation [1, 2, 25]. When she finishes Chapter 12 at hour 15, she buys a $12.99 10-hour audiobook top-up inside the iOS app via external web checkout [24]. The 2025 Epic v. Apple ruling enabled that flow, bypassing Apple's 30% in-app commission [24]. In October and November 2026, Spotify expanded audiobook access toward 180+ markets and rolled out AI-assisted Audiobook Creation Tools across 21 additional markets with Spanish-language support [2].

2. Ad-Supported Segment (9.2% of 9M 2026 Revenue; 17.1% Gross Margin): The free tier serves 499 million ad-supported MAUs out of 788 million total MAUs in Q3 2026, up 12% YoY [2]. It offers shuffle-based mobile music and on-demand podcast and video-podcast playback [2]. Spotify monetizes those streams with audio, video, and display ads sold directly and through automated channels like Spotify Ad Exchange and Ad Studio [2]. Crucially, Ad-Supported is Spotify's zero-CAC acquisition funnel, historically driving over 60% of gross Premium subscriber additions [1]. Beneath Q3 2026's 10% YoY headline growth to €482M (18.7% segment gross margin), channel mix diverged sharply [2]. Nine-month 2026 Ad-Supported revenue grew just 2% YoY to €1,313M because direct-sold channel revenue dropped €177M (-€53M in Q3) amid ad-pricing softness [2]. Automated biddable channels offset that drop by adding €211M in 9M 2026 (+€91M in Q3), leaving programmatic scale-up essential to offset direct ad erosion [2].

Concrete End-to-End Example — Ad-Supported Programmatic Campaign: Suppose a regional U.S. beverage chain wants to reach 18–34-year-old commuters during afternoon drive time. It wants to avoid high television or broad social-media CPMs. Its agency logs into Spotify Ad Studio or Spotify Ad Exchange and sets a $25,000 automated audio-plus-display campaign [2]. The buyer targets by age, metro ZIP code, and mood playlists like 'Workout' and 'Evening Commute', then uploads a 30-second audio spot [2]. Spotify inserts the ad between tracks for free-tier listeners in those metros and logs over 90% completion on non-skippable audio. The platform then settles the impression programmatically. Because Spotify pays lower royalties on free-tier streams and cut fixed podcast minimums in 2023–2024, that €482M quarterly stream now earns a 17–18.7% gross margin [1, 2]. In FY2023, that same segment margin stood at just 3.7% [1].

3. Two-Sided Marketplace (Spotify Campaign Kit — Discovery Mode, Marquee & Showcase): Spotify does not report Marketplace as a separate GAAP segment [1]. Instead, these tools sit inside Cost of Revenue and Premium gross-margin gains [1, 21, 22, 23]. They convert label and artist marketing budgets into high-margin platform revenue or direct royalty rebates [1, 21, 22, 23]. Every day, tens of thousands of new tracks hit Spotify, creating a fierce discovery bottleneck for all artists [21]. Spotify monetizes that bottleneck with three Campaign Kit products [21, 22, 23]. Marquee sells full-screen new-release cards at $0.30–$0.85 CPC on $100–$10,000 budgets [21]. Showcase sells persistent Home and Browse banners for catalog or new releases [23]. Discovery Mode requires zero upfront cash; artists accept a 30% royalty cut on incremental streams in Radio, Autoplay, and personalized Mixes [22].

Concrete End-to-End Example — Independent Artist Using Campaign Kit: Imagine an indie-pop artist with 60,000 monthly listeners releasing a five-track EP. On release week, her distributor launches a $500 Marquee campaign inside Spotify for Artists [21]. It targets lapsed fans who streamed her prior album in the past 12 months [21]. At an average $0.45 CPC, 1,111 warm listeners click into the EP, yielding a 28% save rate [21]. Thirty days later, she enrolls the lead single in Discovery Mode across Radio and Autoplay [22]. Spotify's algorithm boosts the track in passive lean-back sessions. On those incremental streams, Spotify pays 70% of the standard recording royalty rate instead of 100% [22]. That captures a 30% gross-margin rebate at near-zero serving cost [22]. Both sides win: the artist grows her touring base, and Spotify lifts consolidated gross margin above 33% [1, 2, 22].

web_blocks.title: SEGMENT QUALITY TAKEAWAY
paragraphs: Spotify's core is a 91%-revenue, 34.7%-gross-margin recurring subscription business (Premium). A self-funding Ad-Supported tier (17–18% gross margin) feeds the top of the funnel. A zero-inventory-risk Marketplace layer (Discovery Mode, Marquee, Showcase) structurally lifts margins on top.

book_paragraphs: To read Spotify's financial statements properly, you and I have to look past the two clean labels at the top of the segment table—Premium and Ad-Supported—and see the four distinct economic engines humming underneath. On paper, Spotify is simple: 90.8 percent of its €14.28 billion in nine-month 2026 revenue came from Premium subscriptions, and 9.2 percent came from advertising. In reality, those two segments interact in a way that makes Spotify fundamentally different from a pure subscription service like Netflix or a pure ad network like Meta.

Start with Premium, which generated €15.35 billion in 2025 and €12.97 billion through the first nine months of 2026, earning a 34.7 percent gross margin. Think about a real customer you probably know—maybe even yourself. Imagine a U.S. subscriber paying $12.99 a month for an Individual Premium plan. She uses Spotify for forty-five hours a month: AI DJ and daylist on her morning commute, 24-bit Lossless FLAC audio on her speakers, and ten hours of a bestselling audiobook during weekend errands. Because she taps into that 15-hour monthly audiobook allowance, Spotify treats her subscription as a multi-content bundle rather than a music-only plan. That design lowers the statutory mechanical royalty base on the music side—though as we examine in Chapter 3, the Mechanical Licensing Collective is still contesting that bundle valuation in court. And when she hits hour fifteen and buys an extra ten-hour audiobook top-up via web checkout, Spotify captures incremental margin—now reinforced by its late-2026 rollout of 350,000-plus audiobooks across 180-plus markets and AI audiobook creation tools in 21 new countries.

Now look at the second engine: Ad-Supported, which brought in €1.84 billion in 2025 and €1.31 billion in the first nine months of 2026. If you judged Ad-Supported solely on its standalone profit, you would have dismissed it in 2023, when its gross margin was a microscopic 3.7 percent. After stripping out bloated podcast guarantees and automating ad sales, Ad-Supported gross margin rose to 18.0 percent in 2025 and 18.7 percent in Q3 2026. Still, look closely at the nine-month 2026 channel mix: automated programmatic revenue surged €211 million, yet legacy direct-sold ads fell €177 million amid pricing softness, holding nine-month segment growth to just two percent. Even so, Spotify keeps 499 million ad-supported listeners on the platform because the free tier is its zero-cost customer acquisition machine. More than sixty percent of Premium subscribers start as free users who build playlists, train the algorithm, and eventually pay to remove the ads.

To see how Ad-Supported works on the ground, picture a regional coffee or beverage chain trying to reach twenty-something commuters during afternoon drive time. Instead of buying expensive local radio or scattershot social video, its media buyer logs into Spotify Ad Studio, sets a $25,000 budget targeting specific metro ZIP codes and 'Evening Commute' playlists, and launches a thirty-second audio spot with a clickable companion banner. Spotify inserts that ad into a non-skippable break for free-tier listeners, delivers over ninety percent completion, and bills programmatically. Every euro of programmatic ad revenue now drops eighteen cents of gross profit to Spotify—meaning the top-of-funnel marketing machine actually pays for itself.

The third and fourth engines—spoken-word video podcasts and the Two-Sided Marketplace—are where Spotify's margin expansion above 33 percent really comes from. Inside Spotify for Artists, management built a suite called Campaign Kit with three tools: Marquee, Showcase, and Discovery Mode. Picture an independent pop artist with 60,000 monthly listeners dropping a new EP. She spends $500 on a Marquee full-screen recommendation card aimed at fans who streamed her last record, paying roughly forty-five cents per click to drive saves on release week. A month later, she switches on Discovery Mode for her lead single. She pays zero cash up front; instead, she agrees to a thirty-percent reduction in her recording royalty rate on any incremental streams Spotify's algorithm generates in Radio and Autoplay.

Pause and appreciate the elegance of Discovery Mode from Spotify's side of the table. Tens of thousands of tracks are uploaded every single day, and artists are desperate to cut through the noise. By letting artists trade thirty percent of passive-listening royalties for algorithmic amplification, Spotify creates a high-margin Marketplace rebate with virtually zero incremental server cost. Put all four engines together, and you see why consolidated gross margin climbed 750 basis points in under three years—from 25.6 percent in 2023 to 33.1 percent in the first nine months of 2026.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Do not mistake Ad-Supported's 9% revenue share for irrelevance. It is the funnel that keeps Premium's customer acquisition cost low, while Marketplace tools turn the supply side of the music industry into a gross-margin tailwind.
bullets: Premium (90.8% of 9M 2026 revenue) expanded gross margin from 28.8% in FY2023 to 34.7% in 9M 2026.
Ad-Supported (9.2% of 9M 2026 revenue) lifted gross margin from 3.7% in FY2023 to 18.0% in FY2025 and 18.7% in Q3 2026.
Discovery Mode's 30% royalty commission on algorithmic Radio/Autoplay streams is pure gross-margin accretion.
